title: Surface Integrals in Mechanics
short_intro: A surface integral evaluates the scalar or vector field over a two-dimensional surface embedded in a three-dimensional space. In mechanics, it fundamentally describes continuous distributions of forces, such as fluid pressure or gravitational forces, acting across boundaries.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Evaluation of simple surface integrals over planar surfaces, flux of a vector field across coordinate planes, and fundamental definitions of divergence and curl.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Application of the Divergence Theorem (Gauss's Law) to gravitational and electric fields, evaluation of surface integrals over curved surfaces like spheres and cylinders, and tensor formulations.

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Parameterization of Surfaces
bullets: A surface S in three-dimensional space is parameterized by two variables u and v such that r(u, v) = x(u, v)i + y(u, v)j + z(u, v)k.
The differential area vector dS is given by the cross product of the partial derivatives: dS = (r<sub>u</sub> x r<sub>v</sub>) dudv.
The magnitude of the differential area vector represents the scalar differential area element dA = |r<sub>u</sub> x r<sub>v</sub>| dudv.

concept_notes.heading: Surface Integral of a Scalar Field
bullets: Given a scalar function f(x, y, z) defined over a surface S, the surface integral is written as the double integral over the parameter domain D: double-integral f(x, y, z) dA.
It is used in mechanics to calculate the total mass of a thin curved shell or lamina with a variable surface mass density sigma(x, y, z).
The SI unit of a scalar surface integral depends on the integrand, for instance, kg for mass when integrating density over area (m<sup>2</sup>).

concept_notes.heading: Surface Integral of a Vector Field (Flux)
bullets: The flux Psi of a vector field F across an oriented surface S is defined as the surface integral of the normal component of F: Psi = double-integral F dot dS.
Physical significance includes mass flow rate in fluid dynamics and electric or gravitational flux passing through a closed or open boundary.
For closed surfaces, the outward drawn normal is universally chosen as the positive orientation convention.

concept_notes.heading: Physical Applications in Mechanics
bullets: Hydrostatic pressure force on a submerged curved surface is computed by integrating the pressure vector p n over the surface area.
Gauss's Divergence Theorem connects the volume integral of the divergence of a vector field to the surface integral enclosing that volume.
Central force fields, such as Newtonian gravity, obey inverse-square laws directly analyzed via closed surface flux integrals.

derivations.title: Differential Area Vector for an Explicit Surface z = f(x, y)
derivations.conditions: Surface is smooth and explicitly given by z = f(x, y) over a domain D in the xy-plane.
steps: Parameterize the surface using x and y as parameters: r(x, y) = xi + yj + f(x, y)k.
Compute the partial derivative with respect to x: r<sub>x</sub> = i + 0j + (df/dx)k.
Compute the partial derivative with respect to y: r<sub>y</sub> = 0i + j + (df/dy)k.
Calculate the cross product r<sub>x</sub> x r<sub>y</sub> = - (df/dx)i - (df/dy)j + k.
Write the differential area vector dS incorporating the outward or upward orientation.
derivations.result: dS = (- \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} i - \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} j + k) dx dy

derivations.title: Gauss's Divergence Theorem Formulation
derivations.conditions: V is a bounded volume enclosed by a smooth, piecewise continuous closed orientable surface S.
steps: Consider a vector field F = F_x i + F_y j + F_z k with continuous first-order partial derivatives inside volume V.
Express the net outward flux across the bounding surface S as the sum of surface integrals across all components.
Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus in three dimensions relating volume integration of partial derivatives to boundary surface integrals.
Combine the three coordinate components into the divergence operator div F = nabla dot F.

formula_sheet.name: Scalar Surface Integral
formula_sheet.equation_html: \iint_S f(x, y, z) dA = \iint_D f(r(u, v)) |r_u \times r_v| du dv
formula_sheet.variables: f = scalar field, A = surface area, r = position vector
formula_sheet.conditions: Surface must be parameterized and smooth

formula_sheet.name: Vector Surface Integral (Flux)
formula_sheet.variables: F = vector field, n = unit normal vector, dS = vector area element
formula_sheet.units: Units of F multiplied by m^2

formula_sheet.name: Area Element for Explicit Surface
formula_sheet.equation_html: dA = \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} dx dy

formula_sheet.name: Divergence Theorem
formula_sheet.variables: F = vector field, V = volume, S = boundary surface

formula_sheet.name: Hydrostatic Force on a Surface
formula_sheet.variables: p = pressure, n = inward/outward unit normal

formula_sheet.name: Gravitational Flux (Gauss's Law for Gravity)
formula_sheet.variables: g = gravitational field, G = universal gravitational constant, M = mass

formula_sheet.name: Unit Normal Vector Definition
formula_sheet.variables: r_u, r_v = tangent vectors along parameter curves

solved_numericals.question: Evaluate the scalar surface integral double-integral z dA where S is the portion of the plane x + y + z = 1 located in the first octant.
solution_steps: Write the surface equation explicitly as z = 1 - x - y.
Compute partial derivatives: dz/dx = -1 and dz/dy = -1.
Calculate the differential area element dA: dA = sqrt(1 + (-1)^2 + (-1)^2) dx dy = sqrt(3) dx dy.
Set up the limits for the projection D in the xy-plane: x ranges from 0 to 1, y ranges from 0 to 1 - x.
Evaluate the double integral: int_{0}^{1} int_{0}^{1-x} (1 - x - y) sqrt(3) dy dx = sqrt(3) / 6.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the surface flux of the vector field F = xi + yj + zk across the closed surface of a sphere of radius R centered at the origin.
solution_steps: Identify the vector field F = r.
Compute the divergence of F: nabla dot F = d/dx(x) + d/dy(y) + d/dz(z) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.
Apply the Divergence Theorem: flux = triple-integral (nabla dot F) dV = triple-integral 3 dV.
Recognize that the triple integral of 1 dV over the sphere is the volume of the sphere: V = (4/3) pi R^3.
Multiply the volume by the divergence value: 3 * (4/3) pi R^3 = 4 pi R^3.

solved_numericals.question: Evaluate the surface integral double-integral F dot dS where F = 2xz i + dy j + yz k over the surface S of the cube bounded by x = 0, x = 1, y = 0, y = 1, z = 0, z = 1.
solution_steps: Use the Divergence Theorem since S is a closed surface enclosing the unit cube V.
Find the divergence of F: nabla dot F = d/dx(2xz) + d/dy(y) + d/dz(yz) = 2z + 1 + y.
Set up the triple integral over the region V where x, y, z all range from 0 to 1.
Integrate with respect to z, y, and x: int_{0}^{1} int_{0}^{1} int_{0}^{1} (2z + y + 1) dz dy dx.
Evaluate inner integral w.r.t z: [z^2 + yz + z]_{0}^{1} = 1 + y + 1 = y + 2.
Evaluate middle integral w.r.t y: int_{0}^{1} (y + 2) dy = [y^2/2 + 2y]_{0}^{1} = 1/2 + 2 = 5/2.
Evaluate outer integral w.r.t x: int_{0}^{1} (5/2) dx = 5/2.

assumptions_and_limitations: Surfaces must be piecewise smooth, possessing a unique tangent plane and continuous normal vector almost everywhere.
Vector fields must be continuously differentiable within the region of integration for differential theorems to hold.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Confusing the surface integral of a vector field (flux) with the scalar surface area calculation.
common_misconceptions.correct: Scalar surface integrals sum scalar values over area (yielding mass or total scalar quantity), whereas vector surface integrals compute net flux accounting for directional alignment via dot product.
common_misconceptions.why: The dot product with the normal vector introduces directional dependence in flux integrals.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Forgetting the Jacobian square root factor when converting surface integrals to standard xy or uv parameter coordinates.
common_misconceptions.correct: The area element dA must include the magnitude of the cross product of tangent vectors |r_u x r_v|.
common_misconceptions.why: Stretching of the parameter coordinate grid alters differential area magnitudes.

quick_revision: Surface integrals evaluate fields across 2D boundaries; scalar integrals yield quantities like mass, while vector integrals yield flux.
Scalar Surface Integral: \iint_S f(x, y, z) dA = \iint_D f(r(u, v)) |r_u \times r_v| du dv
Vector Surface Integral (Flux): \Psi = \iint_S F \cdot dS = \iint_S (F \cdot n) dA
